title: Walk the same path in four seasons
description: Choose one short path and walk it once in each season, notebook in hand, noting what changed. A year of four slow walks teaches you a place the way residents know it and visitors never do.

body.heading: Set up the year's four walks
paragraphs: Pick a path you can walk in twenty minutes — a park loop, a lane, a stretch of towpath. Mark four dates roughly three months apart. On each walk, take the same notebook and answer the same five prompts: first flower or leaf I see; loudest sound; a smell; something animals are doing; one thing that was not here last time.
Photograph the same tree or view from the same spot each time. Four frames, one year: the cheapest time-lapse you will ever make.

body.heading: What the comparison teaches
paragraphs: Scientists who record seasonal timings — first buds, first migrants, first frost — call the study phenology, and long records of exactly these notes now help track how the climate is shifting. Your four pages are the same instrument, at garden scale.
Most people are surprised less by spring than by how much happens in winter: buds swelling, birdsong starting in February, the path's quiet machinery already running.

takeaway: Walk one short path once per season with the same five prompts and the same photo spot — four slow walks that teach you a place deeply.
materials: A phone or camera for one repeated photo (optional)
supervision: Walk with a companion or tell someone your route; children stay within sight of their adult.
safetyNotes: Dress for the season and check the forecast; shorten or postpone the walk in ice, lightning or extreme heat.
Stay on the path and take care on wet leaves, mud and ice.
